passage: Omkar, it's Saurabh. When you joked yesterday that Divya's bad mood was "hormones", I winced, because I used to say that too. Last year, whenever my girlfriend Meenal got upset, I'd think, oh, it's her cycle, and wait for it to pass. One evening she was angry that I had cancelled dinner with her parents at the last minute. I asked, "Is this a period thing?" She went completely quiet. Then she said, "No. It's a you-cancelled-on-my-parents thing." She was right. I had used her body as an excuse not to listen. Now I just ask, "How are you feeling? What's going on?" Sometimes it's cramps and she wants the hot water bottle. Sometimes it's something I did. Everyone's different. And honestly, we talk a lot more now.

qa.q: What had Saurabh cancelled at the last minute?
qa.a: Dinner with Meenal's parents.

qa.q: How did Meenal feel when Saurabh asked if it was a period thing?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and angry, going completely quiet before naming the real issue.

qa.q: What does Saurabh do differently now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Saurabh asks how Meenal is feeling and what is going on instead of blaming her cycle, which keeps honest talk open.

qa.q: What might change for Omkar after hearing this story?
qa.a: Omkar might think twice before calling Divya's mood "hormones" and ask what is actually bothering her instead.

grounding: Shows a partner learning to ask how she feels instead of blaming every mood on her cycle, since dismissing real concerns as hormones shuts down honest talk.

passage: I'm Sarika, and I've shared a canteen table with Simran and Dia since first year. On Monday Dia arrived late, dumped her bag and snapped, "I'm not doing the slides again." Kunal from our project group laughed. "Uh-oh. Someone's hormonal." A couple of people giggled. I didn't know what to say. Simran did. "Don't do that, Kunal. You don't know what's going on." Then she turned to Dia. "What's up?" Dia's eyes filled. "I've made the slides three times and nobody even says thanks." Nothing to do with hormones at all. Simran helped her split the work fairly, and Kunal quietly offered to do the next set. I've thought about it since. I would have laughed along.

qa.q: What did Dia refuse to do again?
qa.a: The slides.

qa.q: What was Dia feeling when she arrived?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and unappreciated, having made the slides three times without thanks.

qa.q: What did Simran do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She stopped the "hormonal" joke and asked Dia what was wrong, which uncovered a real concern about unfair work.

qa.q: How does Sarika look back on the moment?
qa.a: Sarika admits to having nearly laughed along, and has kept thinking about Simran's response since.

grounding: Illustrates a friend refusing to blame someone's mood on hormones and asking how she is, which brings a real concern into the open.

passage: Beta, you said your friend blames every bad mood of his girlfriend on hormones. Let me tell you about your grandfather. When I came to his house as a bride of nineteen, I was quiet for days at a time. His brothers laughed and said, "Bhabhi's in her monthly mood." Some months I was tired, that's true. But one evening Jagdish found me by the well, and instead of joining their joke, he asked, "What's really wrong?" I told him: my mother was ill back in the village, and nobody had let me visit. He took me on the bus the very next morning. In fifty years he never once said hormones to me. He asked. That is why your Nirmala Dadi still keeps his photo by her bed. So tell your friend to ask.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish find Nirmala?
qa.a: By the well.

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling during those quiet days?
qa.a: She was worried and sad about her mother's illness, and hurt at being mocked.

qa.q: What choice did Jagdish make that mattered?
qa.a: Instead of joining the joke, he asked what was really wrong, then took her to see her mother the next morning.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's brothers see Nirmala's quietness?
qa.a: They dismissed it as her monthly mood, missing her real worry.

grounding: Shows a husband who asks how his wife feels instead of blaming her moods on her cycle, and the honest talk that follows.

passage: The hackathon deadline was midnight, the hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping in the storm, and Chandrika had been coding for six hours straight. When Karan announced he had "handled the slides" and went off to sleep, she slammed her laptop shut. "I'm doing the whole backend alone!" Karan rolled his eyes at Chaitanya. "Relax, it's probably her hormones." Chaitanya didn't laugh. He pulled a chair over. "Ignore that. What's going on?" Chandrika took a breath. "I've written ninety percent of the code, and he gets to present it. I'm tired and I'm angry, and I'm right to be." Chaitanya checked the commit log. She was right. "Then let's fix it. I'll take the database part, and you present tomorrow." At 11:52 they submitted. The next morning Chandrika presented, and Karan quietly apologised.

passage: In their Hyderabad flat, Parul slammed the laptop shut and pushed away her plate. Their flatmate Rohan laughed from the sofa. 'Must be that time of the month.' Lavanya saw Parul's jaw tighten. 'Rohan, don't,' Lavanya said, and sat down next to Parul. 'What's going on? You seem really upset.' Parul breathed out. 'My manager gave my project to someone else. After I did all the groundwork.' 'That's genuinely unfair,' Lavanya said. 'No wonder you're angry.' Rohan went quiet, then muttered sorry. Later Parul told Lavanya, 'If you'd blamed hormones too, I'd never have told you.'
